content: In most countries, individuals who report prior exposure to antiretroviral (ARV) drugs but do not have documented virological failure are typically restarted on a regimen containing non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). The populations at greatest risk for pretreatment HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) are described in detail, with significant differences observed between drug-naïve individuals and those with prior ARV exposure. Resistance to nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) is also notably higher among individuals with prior ARV exposure across all regions. Data from seven recent national surveys conducted by the World Health Organization (WHO) in lowand middle-income countries reveal a stark contrast in pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs between drug-naïve individuals and those with prior ARV exposure. For example, in Namibia, 9% of drug-naïve individuals exhibited resistance compared to 35% of those with prior exposure. Similarly, in Nicaragua, the rates were 11% versus 76%, in Myanmar 3% versus 16%, and in Cameroon 8% versus 20%. Among children, NNRTI resistance is higher in those with prior exposure to ARV drugs related to prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) compared to ARV-naïve children. This suggests that prior ARV exposure is a risk factor for pretreatment HIVDR across various geographic locations, age groups, and individual characteristics. A systematic review from 2014 to 2017 documented high levels of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs among children initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART), with a median resistance rate of 49% (range: 7–100%). In PMTCT-exposed children, more than 50% exhibited pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs in four out of seven studies. Self-reported prior use of ARV drugs among individuals initiating first-line ART may be underreported to healthcare providers due to fear of stigma and discrimination. However, in some national surveys, the proportion of individuals self-reporting prior ARV use was high, such as 18% in Namibia, 12% in Nicaragua, and 19% in Argentina. A large study in South Africa found that 24% of first-line ART initiators reported prior ARV exposure, with 42% of them exhibiting pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs compared to 11% among ARV-naïve individuals. Studies have also reported high rates of first-line ART reinitiation after periods of disengagement from care. For instance, in a South African township, one-quarter of individuals receiving ART disengaged from treatment at least once during a two-year study period. Prior ARV exposure is associated with poorer responses to ART. In Malawi, 24% of individuals who reinitiated NNRTI-based ART after treatment interruption experienced virological failure within three months and had detectable NNRTI resistance. The public health response to pretreatment HIVDR includes updated guidelines recommending the use of non-NNRTI-based regimens for individuals with pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs. This recommendation is based on evidence showing that individuals with pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs initiating NNRTI-based regimens are over 30% less likely to achieve virological suppression, 23 times more likely to experience virological failure or death, and nine times more likely to discontinue treatment compared to those initiating non-NNRTI-based regimens. In Aruba, where HIV is highly endemic, 54% of individuals testing positive for HIV between 2010 and 2015 underwent pretreatment HIVDR testing. The prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs was 32%, prompting changes in local guidelines to prioritize baseline resistance testing and replace WHO-recommended first-line regimens with integrase inhibitor-based regimens. For children, pregnant women, and individuals receiving rifampicin for tuberculosis treatment, the choice of a non-NNRTI-based regimen should consider limited options, age-appropriate formulations, safety, potential drug interactions, and overall principles of drug optimization in ART programs. The systematic review did not identify any other group, apart from those with prior ARV exposure, that was independently characterized by a high risk of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs. The systematic review included 26 studies, comprising randomized controlled trials, case-control studies, and cohort studies. The findings consistently favored the use of non-NNRTI-based regimens for individuals with pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs. However, the certainty of the evidence was downgraded due to indirectness, inconsistency, and imprecision. One clinical trial showed higher risks of virological failure or death, increased treatment discontinuation, and no significant difference in adverse events among individuals with pretreatment HIVDR on NNRTI regimens compared to non-NNRTI regimens. In conclusion, adults and children with pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs initiating NNRTI-based regimens have worse outcomes compared to those initiating non-NNRTI-based regimens. They are less likely to achieve virological suppression, more likely to experience virological failure or death, and more likely to discontinue treatment. These findings underscore the importance of addressing pretreatment HIVDR to ensure the durability and effectiveness of ART regimens.
